tool.name: Scala
tool.tagline: Expressive JVM language fusing functional and object-oriented programming
tool.description: Scala is a statically typed language for the JVM (and JavaScript and native) that combines object-oriented and functional programming with a powerful type system and concise syntax. It powers data and streaming platforms such as Apache Spark, Kafka tooling and Akka/Pekko systems, as well as backend services at many companies. Learning Scala 3 teaches you immutable data modelling, pattern matching, type classes and safe concurrency that carry over to any language.

glossary.def: Java Virtual Machine: the engine that runs Java programs, and Scala programs too, on Windows, macOS and Linux alike.
The tool behind the scala command since Scala 3.5: it compiles, runs, tests and packages Scala code, even single files.
The most widely used build tool for Scala projects: it compiles code, fetches libraries, runs tests and packages the result, configured in a build.sbt file.
In Scala, several lines grouped by indentation or curly braces; its value is the value of its last line.
A Scala for with yield: it walks over one or more collections (or Options, Eithers...) and builds a new one from the results.
A Scala parameter typed => A: the argument is evaluated each time the method uses it (or never), not once before the call.
Scala's automatic conversion of a method into a function value when a function is expected, as in list.foreach(println).
A parameter that accepts any number of arguments, written xs: Int* in Scala; inside the method it is a sequence.
A Scala object with the same name as a class in the same file; the two can see each other's private members, and it usually holds factory methods.
A method whose job is to create objects for you, often checking or adjusting the input first, like Account.empty("bo").
A Scala class marked case for plain data: its fields can't change, == compares contents, and it gets copy, a readable toString and pattern matching for free.
A Scala object marked case: a single fixed value with a readable name, often one option among several.
In Scala pattern matching, a description of a value's shape, like Point(0, y) or (a, b), checked against a value; it can name the parts it matches.
The _ pattern in Scala: it matches anything without giving it a name.
An extra condition on a case, written case n if n < 0 =>; the case only matches if the condition is true.
A Scala type for a value that may be missing: Some(value) when it is there, None when it isn't.
A Scala trait whose subtypes must all be in the same file, so the compiler knows every possible case and can warn when a match misses one.
A type defined as one of a fixed set of alternatives, each possibly carrying its own data, like a Shape that is either a Circle(r) or a Rect(w, h).
The single order Scala puts a class and its traits in, which decides which version of a method runs and what super calls next.
Splitting a function's parameters into separate lists, so giving the first ones returns a function waiting for the rest: add(1)(2).
A function defined only for some inputs, written in Scala as a block of case clauses; collect uses one to filter and transform at once.
A lazy Scala wrapper over a collection: chained operations run item by item, only as far as needed, instead of building a new collection at every step.
A Scala list whose items are computed only when first needed and then remembered, so it can even be infinite.
A lightweight Scala testing library: tests are written as test("name") { ... } blocks with assertEquals checks.
An older, larger Scala testing library offering several styles of writing tests.
A placeholder for a type, written in square brackets like List[A], filled in when the class or method is used.
In Scala, the rule for whether a container of a narrower type (List[Cat]) can be used as a container of a wider one (List[Animal]); marked +A (covariant) or -A (contravariant).
A type that is a more specific kind of another: Cat is a subtype of Animal if every Cat is also an Animal. The wider type is the supertype.
A limit on a type parameter: A <: T (an upper bound) means A must be a subtype of T, and B >: A (a lower bound) means B must be a supertype of A.
On the JVM, type arguments are removed when compiling, so at run time a List[Int] and a List[String] look the same.
In Scala 3, an instance the compiler can pass automatically wherever a matching using parameter is needed: given Ordering[Version] = ...
A Scala parameter list marked using: the compiler fills it in automatically from the givens in scope.
Scala shorthand [A: Show] for "this method needs a given Show[A]".
A capability described by a generic trait, like Show[A] ("can be shown as text"), plus instances for each type that has it; works even for types you don't own.
Where Scala looks for givens besides the code around a call: the companion objects of the types involved.
A method added to an existing type from outside, without changing or wrapping it: extension (s: String) def words = ...
A Scala value that will be available later because the work producing it runs on another thread; it ends with a result or a failure.
The thread pool a Scala Future runs its work on, passed as a using parameter.
A library such as Cats Effect or ZIO that describes work (I/O, concurrency) as values you combine and run later, adding cancellation and safe resource handling.
A popular Scala library for concurrent and asynchronous programs built around a lazy IO value.
A popular Scala library for concurrent, asynchronous and error-aware programs built around a lazy ZIO value.
A Scala 3 type that is the same as another type at run time (say Long) but a separate type for the compiler, so the two can't be mixed up.
A Scala 3 type A | B meaning "a value of type A or of type B".
A Scala 3 type A & B meaning "a value that is both an A and a B".
A Scala method marked inline: the compiler copies its body into every place that calls it, and can resolve inline if and match while compiling.
A Scala 3 type computed by matching on another type, like a match expression that works on types.
A nameless Scala type with a hole, written [X] =>> Either[String, X].
A type parameter that is itself a container type with a hole, like F[_] in trait Functor[F[_]].
Scala 3 macro syntax: '{ ... } turns code into a value the macro can work with, and ${ ... } puts such a value back into code.
Files (.tasty) the Scala 3 compiler writes beside class files, recording every definition with its full types for later compiles, macros and tools.
A compiled .class file the JVM loads and runs, containing bytecode.
Wrapping a simple value such as an Int in an object (java.lang.Integer) so generic code can handle it; it costs memory and time.
Whether code compiled against an old version of a library still runs with a newer version without being recompiled.
A Scala compiler that produces JavaScript, so Scala code can run in web browsers.
A marker starting with @ attached to Scala code, like @main or @throws, that tells the compiler or other tools something about it.

concepts.name: Running Scala and @main
concepts.summary: Run your first Scala 3 program with the scala command, mark where it starts with @main, and try lines out in the REPL.
concepts.why: You need a quick write-and-run routine before you can learn anything else.
concepts.body:
A program is a list of instructions for a computer, written in a **programming language**. Scala is one. It runs on the **JVM** (Java Virtual Machine), the engine that runs Java programs, so Scala works on Windows, macOS and Linux and can use everything written for Java.

Scala code goes in a text file ending in `.scala`. Before it can run, a program called the **compiler** checks the whole file and translates it into a form the JVM can run. This step is called compiling (**compile**). Many mistakes are caught right here, before your program ever starts.

You drive Scala from a **terminal**: a window where you type commands instead of clicking. Since Scala 3.5 the `scala` command is **Scala CLI**, one tool that compiles, runs and tests code. After installing it (for example with Coursier or Homebrew), `scala run hello.scala` compiles and runs a file.

For experiments, `scala repl` (or just `scala`) opens the **REPL**: you type one line, it runs straight away and shows the result. Larger projects use **sbt** instead, a **build tool** that compiles, tests and packages whole projects (covered later).

Every program needs a place to start, its **entry point**. In Scala you mark it with `@main`. The example below defines a **method**, a named piece of code (a later lesson covers methods in full): `@main def greet(name: String, times: Int)` starts the program with two inputs, a piece of text called `name` and a whole number called `times`.

Those inputs come from the **command-line arguments**, the extra words typed after the command: `scala run greet.scala -- Ana 2`. The `--` separates your program's words from Scala CLI's own options. If someone types `abc` where a number belongs, Scala prints a clear error message instead of starting.

Scala 3 uses indentation (spaces at the start of a line) to show which lines belong together, like an outline. Older Scala code uses curly braces `{ }` instead; both work. An `end` marker such as `end greet` can close a long section.

Lines starting with `//` are comments: notes for humans that the compiler skips. Special comments starting `//> using` configure Scala CLI: `//> using scala 3.7` picks the Scala version, and `//> using dep ...` adds a **library** (ready-made code someone else wrote), so one file can be a complete program.

Files ending in `.sc` are **scripts**: their lines simply run from top to bottom, no `@main` needed. The short examples in these lessons without `@main` are written that way, or you can paste them into the REPL.
takeaways: `scala run file.scala` compiles and runs; `scala` alone opens the REPL
`@main` marks where a program starts; its inputs are the words typed after the command
Indentation and curly braces are both valid Scala 3
`//> using` lines choose the Scala version and add libraries
pitfalls: Forgetting `--` before your program's inputs, so Scala CLI tries to treat them as its own options.

quiz.q: @main def run(n: Int) is started with the argument abc. What happens?
options: The program crashes with a long technical report
Scala prints a clear error saying abc is not a valid Int
quiz.explain: Scala generates code that reads the arguments and reports ones that don't fit with a readable error.

quiz.q: What does the compiler do?
options: Checks your code and translates it into a form the JVM can run
Runs each line as you type it
quiz.explain: Compiling happens before the program runs, which is why many mistakes are caught early.

concepts.name: Values, variables and types
concepts.summary: Name values with val and var, meet Scala's basic types, let the compiler work types out, and put values into text.
concepts.why: Values that never change and types checked before the program runs shape all Scala code.
concepts.body:
A program needs to remember things. `val x = 10` gives the value 10 the name `x`. A `val` can never get a different value later: it is **immutable** (unchangeable). `var y = 10` creates a **variable** whose value you can change: `y = 11`. Scala programmers use `val` almost everywhere, because values that never change are easier to follow.

Every value has a type, the kind of thing it is, which decides what you can do with it (its **data type**). Scala checks types when it compiles, before the program runs, so adding a number to a yes/no value is caught early. Languages that check like this are called **statically typed**.

You rarely have to write types yourself: Scala works them out, so `val x = 10` is an `Int`. This is **type inference**. You can still write the type after a colon, `val ratio: Double = 0.5`; that is a **type annotation**, good practice wherever the type isn't obvious.

The basic types:

- `Int` for whole numbers (**integers**) like `42`; `Long` for very large ones; `BigInt` for any size.
- `Double` for numbers with a decimal point (**floating-point numbers**), like `3.14`.
- `Boolean` for `true` or `false`, and `Char` for one character, written `'a'`.
- `String` for text in double quotes, like `"Ada"`.
- `Unit`, written `()`, means "no useful value"; `println` gives back `Unit`.

Every value is an **object**: a thing with built-in abilities, called **methods**, that you use with a dot. `"abc".reverse` gives `"cba"`, and `1.to(5)` gives the numbers 1 to 5.

Dividing one `Int` by another gives an `Int` and throws the remainder away: `7 / 2` is `3`. This is **integer division**; write `7 / 2.0` to get `3.5`.

**String interpolation** puts values into text: `s"Hi $name, ${a + b}"` (note the `s` before the opening quote). `f"$pi%.2f"` shows a number with two decimals. Triple quotes `"""..."""` hold text over several lines, and `.stripMargin` removes the `|` used to line it up.

`==` asks whether two values are equal, so `"ab" == "a" + "b"` is `true`. The rarer `eq` asks whether they are the very same object.

All types fit in one family tree: `Any` at the top, then `AnyVal` (number-like types such as `Int`) and `AnyRef` (all other objects). At the bottom sits `Nothing`, the type of code that never finishes normally, such as code that stops with an error.
concepts.code:
val name = "Ada"
var visits = 1
visits += 1                               // same as visits = visits + 1
// name = "Bob"            // error: Reassignment to val name

val pi: Double = math.Pi                  // with a type annotation
val big = BigInt(2).pow(100)
println(s"$name visited $visits times")   // Ada visited 2 times
println(f"pi is $pi%.3f")                 // pi is 3.142
println(s"2^100 has ${big.toString.length} digits")  // 2^100 has 31 digits

val a = "scala"
val b = "sca" + "la"
println(a == b)                           // true (same text)
println(7 / 2)                            // 3 (integer division)
println(7 / 2.0)                          // 3.5
println("""|multi
           |line""".stripMargin)          // multi / line
takeaways: Prefer `val`; use `var` only when a value really has to change
Types are checked before the program runs, and usually worked out for you
`s"..."` puts values into text; `f"..."` formats numbers
`==` compares values
pitfalls: Integer division: `7 / 2` is 3; make one of the numbers a Double, like `7 / 2.0`, to get 3.5.

quiz.q: What happens when you give a val a new value?
options: An error when compiling, before the program runs
quiz.explain: A val can't be changed, and the compiler rejects the code.

quiz.q: In Scala, what does "ab" == "a" + "b" give?
quiz.explain: == compares contents, so two strings with the same text are equal.

concepts.name: Expressions and control structures
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if, repeat work with while and for, and see why almost everything in Scala produces a value.
concepts.why: Thinking of code as expressions that produce values, rather than steps, is what makes Scala code short.
concepts.body:
Programs make decisions: if a number is below zero, say "negative", otherwise "positive". Code that runs only when a condition holds is a **conditional**: `if x < 0 then "negative" else "positive"`. Conditions use comparisons like `<`, `>`, `==` (equal) and `!=` (not equal), combined with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not).

In Scala nearly everything is an **expression**: a piece of code that produces a value. So the result of an `if` can be stored directly: `val sign = if x < 0 then -1 else 1`. Many languages also have **statements**, instructions that do something but produce no value; Scala mostly doesn't need them.

A **block** is several lines grouped together, by indentation or by `{ }`. Its value is the value of its last line, which is how `total` in the example gets 42. An `if` without an `else` has nothing to give when the condition is false, so its value is `()`, "no useful value".

A **loop** repeats code:

- `while n < 100 do n *= 3` repeats as long as the condition holds (`n *= 3` means `n = n * 3`).
- `for i <- 1 to 5 do println(i)` runs once for each number from 1 to 5. Each pass is one **iteration**.
- `1 to 5` includes 5, `1 until 5` stops before it, and `by` sets the step: `10 to 1 by -3`.

A `for` can walk over two ranges at once and skip some combinations with an `if`: `for i <- 1 to 3; j <- 1 to 3 if i != j do ...`.

With `yield` instead of `do`, a `for` collects its results into a new collection: `for k <- 1 until 5 yield k * k` gives `Vector(1, 4, 9, 16)`. This is a **for comprehension** (also called a for expression). (A **Vector** is a list-like collection; collections get their own lesson.)

`match` is the other key structure: `x match { case 1 => "one"; case _ => "many" }` picks a result by comparing `x` with each `case`, where `_` means "anything else". A later lesson covers it in depth.

There is no `break` or `continue`. Usually a method such as `find` (first item that fits) or `exists` (is there any?) says what you want more clearly, and `scala.util.boundary` offers `break` for the rare early exit. `try`/`catch`, which handles errors, produces a value too, and a method rarely needs `return`: its last expression is its result.
concepts.code:
val x = -7
val sign = if x < 0 then "negative" else "non-negative"
println(sign)                               // negative

val total =
  val a = 10
  val b = 32
  a + b                                     // last line: the block's value
println(total)                              // 42

var n = 1
while n < 100 do n *= 3
println(n)                                  // 243

for i <- 1 to 3; j <- 1 to 3 if i < j do
  print(s"($i,$j) ")                        // (1,2) (1,3) (2,3)
println()

val squares = for k <- 1 until 5 yield k * k
println(squares)                            // Vector(1, 4, 9, 16)
println((10 to 1 by -3).toList)             // List(10, 7, 4, 1)
takeaways: `if`, blocks, `match`, `try` and `for ... yield` all produce values
`1 to n` includes n; `1 until n` stops before it
`for ... do` repeats actions; `for ... yield` builds a new collection
pitfalls: Writing an `if` without `else` and expecting a useful value: when the condition is false the result is `()`.

quiz.q: What is the type of if (cond) 42 with no else?
options: Unit or Any depending on cond
quiz.explain: Without else, the missing case gives Unit; the nearest type in the family tree that covers both Int and Unit is AnyVal.

quiz.q: How many times does for i <- 1 until 4 do println(i) print?
quiz.explain: until stops before 4, so i takes the values 1, 2 and 3.

concepts.name: Methods and function values
concepts.summary: Write your own methods with def, use default and named arguments, and pass functions around as values.
concepts.why: Methods let you name and reuse work, and passing functions as values is the basis of how Scala handles collections of data.
concepts.body:
A method is a named piece of code you can run again and again. Define one with `def`:

```scala
def area(w: Double, h: Double = 1.0): Double = w * h
```

`w` and `h` are its **parameters**: named inputs, each with a type. `: Double` after the parentheses is the type of the result, and the expression after `=` computes it.

Calling `area(3, 2)` passes the **arguments** 3 and 2, and the method gives back 6.0, its **return value**. Parameter types are required; the result type can usually be inferred, but write it on methods other code uses.

Because `h` has a **default value**, `area(3)` also works. Callers can name their arguments and give them in any order: `area(h = 2, w = 3)`. These are **named arguments**, and they make calls easy to read.

A method can take several parameter lists: `def add(a: Int)(b: Int) = a + b`, called as `add(1)(2)`. This lets the last input be a block of code, so calls look like built-in structures: `retry(3) { ... }`.

A parameter typed `=> A` is a **by-name parameter**: instead of being worked out before the call, the argument is evaluated each time the method uses it, or never if unused. In the example, `logIf(false) { ... }` never runs its block.

In Scala a **function** is also a value you can store and pass around, like a number. `(x: Int) => x * 2` is a function value, also called a **lambda**: "given x, give back x * 2". Its type is written `Int => Int`.

Passing functions to methods is everywhere: `List(1, 2, 3).map(x => x * 2)` applies the function to each item and gives `List(2, 4, 6)`. When the types are clear, `_` can stand for the input: `map(_ * 2)`. A method like `map` that takes a function is a **higher-order function**.

Where a function is expected and you pass in a method, Scala converts it for you. This is **eta-expansion**, and it is why `names.foreach(println)` just works.

A parameter written `xs: Int*` accepts any number of arguments (**varargs**): `sum(1, 2, 3)`. To pass an existing list, write `sum(list*)`.
concepts.code:
def area(w: Double, h: Double = 1.0): Double = w * h
println(area(3))                        // 3.0
println(area(h = 2, w = 5))             // 10.0

val double: Int => Int = x => x * 2
val add = (a: Int, b: Int) => a + b
println(List(1, 2, 3).map(double))      // List(2, 4, 6)
println(List(1, 2, 3).map(_ + 10))      // List(11, 12, 13)
println(List(4, 5).reduce(add))         // 9 (combines items with add)

def twice(f: Int => Int, x: Int): Int = f(f(x))
println(twice(_ * 3, 2))                // 18

def logIf(enabled: Boolean)(msg: => String): Unit =
  if enabled then println(msg)
logIf(false) { println("never evaluated"); "expensive" }
logIf(true)("cheap")                    // cheap

def sum(xs: Int*): Int = xs.sum
println(sum(1, 2, 3) + sum(List(4, 5)*))  // 15
takeaways: `def` defines methods; named and default arguments keep calls clear
Functions are values: `x => x * 2`, or the shorthand `_ * 2`
`=> A` parameters are by-name: evaluated only when used
Methods turn into functions automatically when one is expected
pitfalls: Using `_` twice and expecting the same input both times: `_ * _` is a function of two separate inputs.

quiz.q: What does List(1, 2).map(_ * _) do?
quiz.explain: Each _ is a separate input, so _ * _ means (a, b) => a * b, which doesn't fit map.

quiz.q: Given def area(w: Double, h: Double = 1.0) = w * h, what is area(4)?
quiz.explain: h falls back to its default value 1.0, so the result is 4.0 * 1.0.

concepts.name: Classes, objects and companions
concepts.summary: Design your own kinds of objects with classes, make single shared objects with object, and pair them as companions.
concepts.why: Classes and objects organise data and the code that works on it in every Scala program.
concepts.body:
So far you have used values that Scala provides. A **class** is a blueprint for your own kind of object: an `Account` class says what every account holds and what it can do. Each object made from it is an **instance**: `Account("ana", 10)` creates one.

The first line of the class lists what's needed to create an instance; that is its **constructor**: `class Account(val owner: String, private var balance: Double)`. Parameters marked `val` become public, read-only **fields** (data stored on each object), `var` makes a changeable field, and a plain parameter is visible only inside the class. In Scala 3 you don't need the word `new`.

Code in the class body runs every time an instance is created, so `require(balance >= 0)` there rejects bad input straight away.

Members are public (usable anywhere) by default. `private` limits one to the class itself, and `protected` also allows classes built on top of this one. Extra constructors (`def this(...)`) exist, but default values usually make them unnecessary.

An object defined with `object Name` is a **singleton**: exactly one of it exists, created the first time it's used. Use one for helper methods, fixed values and the program's starting point.

An object with the same name as a class, in the same file, is that class's **companion object**. The two can see each other's private members. The companion is the usual home for **factory methods**, methods that create instances for you: `Account.empty("bo")` reads better than spelling out the constructor, and a factory can check or adjust the input first.

Methods with one argument can be written without the dot and parentheses: `a max b` means `a.max(b)`. Method names can even be made of signs like `+`: `def +(other: Money)`.

Every object already has a `toString` method that turns it into text. Writing `override def toString = ...` replaces it with your own version; replacing a method you got for free like this is called an **override**.
concepts.code:
class Account(val owner: String, private var balance: Double):
  require(balance >= 0, "negative balance")
  def deposit(amount: Double): Unit = balance += amount
  def current: Double = balance
  override def toString = s"Account($owner, $balance)"

object Account:                       // the companion object
  private var created = 0
  def empty(owner: String): Account = // a factory method
    created += 1
    Account(owner, 0)
  def count: Int = created

object MathUtil:                      // a singleton of helpers
  val Tau = 2 * math.Pi
  def clamp(x: Int, lo: Int, hi: Int) = x max lo min hi

@main def demo(): Unit =
  val a = Account.empty("ana")
  a.deposit(25)
  println(a)                          // Account(ana, 25.0)
  println(a.current)                  // 25.0
  println(Account.count)              // 1
  println(MathUtil.clamp(15, 0, 10))  // 10
  // a.balance                        // error: balance is private
takeaways: Constructor parameters marked `val` or `var` become fields
An `object` is a single shared instance, created on first use
A companion object shares private members with its class and holds factory methods
`new` is optional in Scala 3
pitfalls: Leaving out `val` on a constructor parameter and then trying to read it from outside the class.

quiz.q: class Point(x: Int) declares x without val. Can other code read p.x?
options: Only classes built on Point can
No, it's private to the class
quiz.explain: A parameter without val or var is not a public field; add val to make it readable from outside.

concepts.name: Case classes
concepts.summary: Model plain data with case classes: unchangeable fields, equality by contents, copy, readable printing and taking apart by pattern for free.
concepts.why: Case classes are how Scala represents data: customer details, messages, events and settings.
concepts.code:
case class Point(x: Int, y: Int):
  def +(o: Point): Point = Point(x + o.x, y + o.y)

case class User(name: String, email: String, active: Boolean = true)

val p = Point(1, 2)
val q = Point(1, 2)
println(p == q)                      // true (same contents)
println(p eq q)                      // false (two separate objects)
println(p + Point(10, 10))           // Point(11,12)

val u = User("ana", "ana@example.com")
val inactive = u.copy(active = false)
println(inactive)                    // User(ana,ana@example.com,false)

val seen = Set(p, q, Point(0, 0))
println(seen.size)                   // 2 (p and q count as one)

p match
  case Point(0, y) => println(s"on the y axis at $y")
  case Point(x, y) => println(s"at $x, $y")   // at 1, 2

println(u.productElementNames.toList)  // List(name, email, active)
takeaways: `case class` = unchangeable fields + equality by contents + copy + pattern matching
"Update" with `copy(field = value)`
Safe as Map keys and Set items
Model alternatives with `sealed trait`s or `enum`s, not case classes built on case classes
pitfalls: Giving a case class var fields and using it as a Map key: change a field later and the Map can no longer find it.

quiz.q: case class P(x: Int). What is P(1) == P(1)?
options: true only if both are vals
quiz.explain: Case classes generate == (equals) and hashCode from their field values.

concepts.name: Pattern matching
concepts.summary: Use match to compare a value against patterns: fixed values, types, case classes, tuples, lists and guards.
concepts.why: Pattern matching is Scala's main way to choose what to do based on the shape of data.
concepts.body:
A match expression compares a value against a list of **patterns**, descriptions of what a value might look like, and runs the first `case` that fits: `x match { case pattern => result ... }`. This is **pattern matching**. Like `if`, it is an expression, so it produces a value.

The kinds of pattern:

- Fixed values: `case 0 =>`, `case "quit" =>`.
- A name, or `_`: `case n =>` matches anything and calls it `n`; `case _ =>` matches anything without naming it (a **catch-all pattern**).
- Types: `case s: String =>` matches only text, and inside that case `s` is known to be a `String`.
- Case classes, nested freely: `case Order(id, Customer(name, _)) =>` takes an order apart and names its pieces.
- **Tuples**, small fixed groups of values like `(1, "a")`: `case (a, b) =>`. Lists: `case List(first, rest*) =>` or `case head :: tail =>` separate the first item from the rest.
- One of several: `case 1 | 2 =>`. Naming the whole value while matching its shape: `case p @ Point(0, _) =>`.

A **guard** adds a condition: `case n if n < 0 =>` matches only negative numbers.

If no case matches, the program stops with a `MatchError`. To avoid that, match on a closed set of possibilities (a `sealed trait` or an `enum`, covered later): the compiler then warns you when a case is missing.

Watch out: a lowercase name in a pattern always creates a new name that matches anything. To compare against an existing value instead, put it in backticks (`` case `expected` => ``) or give it a name starting with a capital letter.

Patterns work in other places too. `val (q, r) = (7 / 2, 7 % 2)` splits a pair into two names (`%` gives the remainder), and patterns also appear in `for` loops and in `collect`.
concepts.code:
case class Customer(name: String, vip: Boolean)
case class Order(id: Int, customer: Customer, total: Double)

def describe(x: Any): String = x match
  case 0                         => "zero"
  case n: Int if n < 0           => s"negative int $n"
  case n: Int                    => s"int $n"
  case s: String                 => s"string of length ${s.length}"
  case (a, b)                    => s"pair $a and $b"
  case List(first, rest*)        => s"list starting $first, ${rest.size} more"
  case Order(id, Customer(name, true), _) => s"VIP order $id for $name"
  case _                         => "something else"

println(describe(-4))                         // negative int -4
println(describe("hey"))                      // string of length 3
println(describe((1, "a")))                   // pair 1 and a
println(describe(List(9, 8, 7)))              // list starting 9, 2 more
println(describe(Order(7, Customer("Ana", true), 99.0)))  // VIP order 7 for Ana
println(describe(3.5))                        // something else

val (q, r) = (17 / 5, 17 % 5)
println(s"$q remainder $r")                   // 3 remainder 2
takeaways: Each case is tried in order, top to bottom; the first match wins
Patterns take apart case classes, tuples and lists, with optional guards
Lowercase names create new names; use backticks to compare with an existing value
A value no case matches causes a MatchError
pitfalls: Writing `case expected =>` meaning the existing value `expected`: it creates a new name that matches everything.

quiz.q: val limit = 10; 5 match { case limit => "hit"; case _ => "miss" } returns?
options: "hit", because limit is a new name that matches anything
quiz.explain: A lowercase name in a pattern creates a new name; write `limit` in backticks to compare with the existing value.

concepts.name: Immutable collections
concepts.summary: Keep many values together with List, Vector, Set and Map, and transform them with map, filter and foldLeft.
concepts.why: Collections and the methods that transform them make up most everyday Scala code.
concepts.body:
A collection holds many values together: a list of names, a group of labels, a table of prices. Scala's standard collections are immutable: methods like `map` never change the original. They return a new collection, and the old one stays exactly as it was.

The main kinds:

- `List(5, 3, 8)` is an ordered list. Adding to the front with `::` is instant, but reaching the item at a position means walking past every item before it.
- `Vector` is an ordered sequence where reaching any item by its **index** (position number, counting from 0) is fast. It is the best general-purpose choice.
- `Set` holds values without duplicates.
- `Map` is a lookup table of **key-value pairs**, like a phone book: `Map("ana" -> 31, "bo" -> 25)`.
- `1 to 10` (a Range) and `Array` (a fixed-size sequence whose items can be changed) complete the picture.

All of them share the same methods, most of which take a function:

- `map`, `filter`, `flatMap` and `collect` transform;
- `foldLeft`, `sum`, `max`, `count`, `exists`, `forall` and `find` combine or search;
- `groupBy`, `partition`, `zip`, `sortBy`, `distinct`, `take` and `drop` reshape.

`foldLeft(0)(_ + _)` walks the collection carrying a running result: it starts at 0 and adds each item in turn, which sums the list.

Looking something up may find nothing. `ages.get("cy")` returns an **Option**: `Some(31)` when the key exists or `None` when it doesn't, so you can't forget the missing case. `getOrElse("cy", 0)` gives a fallback, while `ages("cy")` stops with an error if the key is missing. `+` or `updated` returns a new map with an extra entry.

Chaining these methods replaces most loops: you describe what you want instead of how to step through the items. `toList`, `toVector`, `toSet` and `toMap` convert between kinds.
concepts.code:
val nums = List(5, 3, 8, 1)
println(0 :: nums)                          // List(0, 5, 3, 8, 1)
println(nums.map(_ * 2).filter(_ > 5))      // List(10, 6, 16)
println(nums.foldLeft(0)(_ + _))            // 17
println(nums.sorted.take(2))                // List(1, 3)
println(nums.exists(_ > 7))                 // true

val v = Vector("a", "b", "c")
println(v.updated(1, "B"))                  // Vector(a, B, c)
println(v)                                  // Vector(a, b, c) (unchanged)

val ages = Map("ana" -> 31, "bo" -> 25)
println(ages.get("cy"))                     // None
println(ages.getOrElse("cy", 0))            // 0
println(ages + ("cy" -> 40))                // Map(ana -> 31, bo -> 25, cy -> 40)

val words = List("apple", "avocado", "banana", "cherry")
println(words.groupBy(_.head).view.mapValues(_.size).toMap)
// Map(a -> 2, b -> 1, c -> 1) (order may vary)
println(words.partition(_.length > 5))      // (List(avocado, banana, cherry),List(apple))
takeaways: Standard collections never change: methods return new ones
List for adding at the front and walking item by item; Vector for fast access by position
map, filter, foldLeft, groupBy and friends replace loops
`Map.get` returns an Option; `map(key)` stops with an error if the key is missing
pitfalls: Reading `list(i)` inside a loop over a List: each lookup walks from the start, which gets slow. Use a Vector, or loop over the items directly.

quiz.q: Which collection gives fast access to any item by its position?
quiz.explain: Vector reaches any position quickly; a List has to walk from the front.

concepts.name: Traits and mixins
concepts.summary: Describe shared sets of methods with traits, some left for classes to fill in and some ready-made, and mix several traits into one class.
concepts.why: Traits are Scala's main tool for sharing code between classes and for describing what a type can do.
concepts.body:
A **trait** is a named set of methods and values that classes can take on. It can leave some methods abstract, declared without a body for each class to fill in, and provide others ready-made. A class or object **extends** at most one class but any number of traits: `class Duck extends Animal, Swimmer, Flyer` (Scala 3 style; `with` also works). It then gets everything they define; this is **inheritance**.

Use traits to:

- describe an **interface**, a list of methods a type promises to provide without saying how (`trait Repository[A] { def find(id: Long): Option[A] }`; `[A]` makes it work for any item type),
- share behaviour (a `Logging` trait with a concrete `log` method),
- stack changes on top of each other (several traits overriding the same method, each calling `super` to reach the next version).

When multiple traits define the same method, Scala uses **linearization**: the class and its traits are put in a single order (roughly right to left) and `super` calls the next one in that order. This gives predictable behaviour, unlike the ambiguity some languages have when two parents define the same method.

Scala 3 traits can take **parameters** (`trait Greeting(val name: String)`), which only the class that first mixes it in passes.

Use an **abstract class** (a class that can't be created on its own, only extended) instead when Java code must call its constructor, or when a type is clearly a shared base implementation. Otherwise prefer traits.

Mark a trait `sealed` when all implementations live in the same file: then the compiler knows every **subtype** (every type that extends it), so a `match` over it can be checked for a missing case (next lesson).
concepts.code:
trait Shape:
  def area: Double                       // abstract
  def describe: String = f"${getClass.getSimpleName} with area $area%.2f"

trait Logged extends Shape:
  override def describe: String = "[log] " + super.describe

trait Loud extends Shape:
  override def describe: String = super.describe.toUpperCase

class Circle(r: Double) extends Shape:
  def area = math.Pi * r * r

class Square(s: Double) extends Shape, Loud, Logged:
  def area = s * s

trait Greeting(val greeting: String):
  def greet(n: String) = s"$greeting, $n"
object Formal extends Greeting("Good day")

@main def traitsDemo(): Unit =
  println(Circle(1).describe)      // Circle with area 3.14
  println(Square(2).describe)      // [log] SQUARE WITH AREA 4.00
  println(Formal.greet("Ana"))     // Good day, Ana
takeaways: Traits mix abstract and concrete members; a class can extend many
Linearization orders traits; `super` calls the next in line
Scala 3 traits can take parameters
`sealed` traits enable exhaustive matching
pitfalls: Assuming trait order doesn't matter: `extends A, B` and `extends B, A` can behave differently.

quiz.q: Square extends Shape, Loud, Logged, both overriding describe and calling super. Which runs first?
quiz.explain: Linearization puts the rightmost trait first, so Logged runs and its super is Loud.

concepts.name: Enums and algebraic data types
concepts.summary: Model a fixed set of alternatives with enum and sealed traits, and let the compiler check that a match covers them all.
concepts.why: Algebraic data types let the compiler prove you've handled every case, which removes whole families of bugs.
concepts.body:
An **algebraic data type** (ADT) is a type defined as one of a fixed set of alternatives, each possibly carrying data. Scala 3's **enum** (short for enumeration: a type with a fixed set of named values) expresses them directly:

- A simple enumeration: `enum Color { case Red, Green, Blue }` with `Color.values`, `Color.valueOf("Red")` and `ordinal` (its position, counting from 0).
- Enums can have parameters and members: `enum Planet(val mass: Double) { case Earth extends Planet(5.97e24) ... }`.
- Each case can carry its own data, making a full ADT: `enum Shape { case Circle(r: Double); case Rect(w: Double, h: Double) }`.
- Enums can work for any type `A`: the standard `Option` could be written `enum Option[+A] { case Some(x: A); case None }`.

The equivalent in Scala 2 style, still common and sometimes more flexible, is a `sealed trait` with `case class` and `case object` subtypes in the same file.

Because the set of alternatives is closed, a `match` that misses one produces a compiler **warning** ("match may not be exhaustive"). Turn warnings into errors (`-Werror`) and the compiler hands you a checklist whenever a new case is added.

Design tip: make illegal states unrepresentable. Instead of a class with fields that may be empty (`null`) and a text `status` field, define an enum where each case has exactly the data that state needs.
concepts.code:
enum Color:
  case Red, Green, Blue

enum Payment:
  case Card(number: String, expiry: String)
  case Transfer(iban: String)
  case Cash

import Payment.*

def fee(p: Payment, amount: Double): Double = p match
  case Card(_, _)  => amount * 0.02
  case Transfer(_) => 0.5
  case Cash        => 0.0
  // removing a case gives: "match may not be exhaustive"

@main def enums(): Unit =
  println(Color.values.toList)             // List(Red, Green, Blue)
  println(Color.valueOf("Green").ordinal)  // 1
  val payments = List(Card("4242", "12/29"), Transfer("AM00"), Cash)
  println(payments.map(fee(_, 100)))       // List(2.0, 0.5, 0.0)
  println(Transfer("X"))                   // Transfer(X)
takeaways: `enum` models a closed set of cases, with or without data
Sealed traits plus case classes are the equivalent older style
Exhaustiveness checking warns when a case is missing
Make illegal states unrepresentable
pitfalls: Adding a catch-all pattern `case _` to every match, which silences exhaustiveness warnings when new cases are added.

quiz.q: Why prefer an enum over a String status field?
options: The compiler checks that matches handle every case
quiz.explain: A closed enum lets the compiler warn about unhandled cases, which a free-form String can't.

concepts.name: Option, Either and Try
concepts.summary: Represent missing values and failures as ordinary data with Option, Either and Try, instead of null and exceptions.
concepts.why: When failure is part of a method's type, callers can see what can go wrong and must deal with it, and the steps chain together neatly.
concepts.body:
Many languages signal trouble in two ways. **Null** is a special "no value here" that crashes the program when used by mistake. An **exception** is an error that jumps out of the current code until something catches it. Idiomatic Scala avoids `null`, and avoids exceptions for failures you expect. Three types make absence and failure visible instead:

- **Option**: `Option[A]` is `Some(a)` or `None`. Use it for values that may be missing: `map.get(key)`, `list.find(...)`, `headOption`. Wrap Java values that may be null with `Option(x)`.
- **Either**: `Either[E, A]` is `Left(error)` or `Right(value)`. It is right-biased: `map` (transform the value) and `flatMap` (chain a step that itself returns an Either) work on the `Right` and pass a `Left` through unchanged. Use it when the caller needs to know **why** something failed, with a typed error (often an enum).
- **Try**: `Try[A]` is `Success(a)` or `Failure(throwable)`. `Try(expr)` catches ordinary exceptions (not fatal ones like running out of memory), which makes it the bridge from code that throws them, such as many Java libraries.

All three share the same methods: `map`, `flatMap`, `filter`, `getOrElse`, `fold`, `foreach` and conversions like `toOption`, `toEither` and `toRight(err)`. Pattern matching works too.

Don't call `.get` on an `Option` or `Try`: it throws when empty and defeats the purpose. Chain transformations and decide at the edge of the program what to do with the error. Chaining several steps that can fail is cleanest with a `for` comprehension (next lesson).
concepts.code:
import scala.util.{Try, Success, Failure}

val ages = Map("ana" -> 31)
println(ages.get("ana").map(_ + 1))         // Some(32)
println(ages.get("bo").getOrElse(0))        // 0
println(Option(null: String))               // None

enum ParseError:
  case Empty
  case NotANumber(input: String)

def parse(s: String): Either[ParseError, Int] =
  if s.isEmpty then Left(ParseError.Empty)
  else s.toIntOption.toRight(ParseError.NotANumber(s))

println(parse("42").map(_ * 2))             // Right(84)
println(parse("x4").map(_ * 2))             // Left(NotANumber(x4))
println(parse("").fold(e => s"error: $e", n => s"ok $n"))  // error: Empty

val t = Try("12a".toInt)
t match
  case Success(n)  => println(n)
  case Failure(ex) => println(ex.getClass.getSimpleName)  // NumberFormatException
println(Try(10 / 2).toOption)               // Some(5)
takeaways: `Option` for absence, `Either` for typed errors, `Try` to catch exceptions
All support map, flatMap, getOrElse and fold
Either is right-biased: map works on the success value
Never call `.get`; handle the empty case explicitly
pitfalls: Wrapping everything in Try, losing the specific error type that Either with an error enum would give.

quiz.q: What does Left("oops").map((x: Int) => x + 1) return?
quiz.explain: Either is right-biased: map transforms only a Right and passes a Left through unchanged.

concepts.name: For comprehensions
concepts.summary: Chain flatMap, map and withFilter readably over Options, Eithers, collections and similar types.
concepts.why: For comprehensions make step-by-step logic over Options, Eithers and similar wrapper types read like plain sequential code.
concepts.body:
A `for` with `yield`, also called a for comprehension, is a shorter way of writing ("syntactic sugar" for) calls to `flatMap`, `map` and `withFilter`. The compiler rewrites

```scala
for a <- fa; b <- fb(a) yield f(a, b)
```

into `fa.flatMap(a => fb(a).map(b => f(a, b)))`. Any type with those methods works, which is why the same syntax handles collections, `Option`, `Either`, `Try`, `Future` (a value computed in the background, covered later) and the `IO` type of libraries like Cats Effect.

With `Option` and `Either` it expresses "do these steps in order and stop at the first failure": each `<-` unwraps a value, and if any step yields `None` or `Left`, the whole expression stops there and returns it.

Other parts:

- `if cond` guards filter (requires `withFilter`; `Either` doesn't support guards without an empty value).
- `x = expr` binds an intermediate value without unwrapping.
- Each `x <- ...` line is a step. With collections, several steps produce every combination.

All `<-` steps in one comprehension must be of the **same kind**: you can't mix `Option` and `List` steps directly; convert first (`opt.toList`, `opt.toRight(err)`).

Without `yield`, a `for` loop is rewritten into `foreach` and returns `Unit`.
concepts.code:
case class User(id: Int, name: String, managerId: Option[Int])
val users = Map(1 -> User(1, "Ana", None), 2 -> User(2, "Bo", Some(1)))

def managerName(id: Int): Option[String] =
  for
    user    <- users.get(id)
    mgrId   <- user.managerId
    manager <- users.get(mgrId)
  yield manager.name

println(managerName(2))   // Some(Ana)
println(managerName(1))   // None (Ana has no manager)

def toAge(s: String): Either[String, Int] = s.toIntOption.toRight(s"bad: $s")
val total = for
  a <- toAge("30")
  b <- toAge("x")
  sum = a + b
yield sum
println(total)            // Left(bad: x)

val pairs = for n <- List(1, 2, 3); c <- List('a', 'b') if n != 2 yield s"$n$c"
println(pairs)            // List(1a, 1b, 3a, 3b)
takeaways: `for ... yield` is rewritten into flatMap/map/withFilter
Over Option/Either it stops at the first None/Left
All `<-` steps must be the same kind of type
`x = expr` binds a plain intermediate value
pitfalls: Mixing an Option step into a List comprehension (or Future with Option) and getting confusing type errors.

quiz.q: What does for { a <- Some(1); b <- None: Option[Int] } yield a + b return?
quiz.explain: The second step is None, so flatMap short-circuits and the result is None.

concepts.name: Higher-order functions and currying
concepts.summary: Write functions that take or return functions, split parameters into separate lists (currying) and combine behaviour.
concepts.why: Higher-order functions remove duplication and are the core of functional design in Scala.
concepts.body:
A **higher-order function** takes a function as a parameter or returns one. `map`, `filter` and `foldLeft` are examples; writing your own lets you pass in behaviour, not just values (`[A]` lets them work for any result type): `def retry[A](n: Int)(action: => A): A`, `def timed[A](label: String)(body: => A): A`.

Returning functions builds behaviour from parts: `def multiplier(k: Int): Int => Int = x => x * k`. The returned function is a **closure**: it remembers `k` from where it was created.

**Currying** means splitting parameters into separate lists: `def add(a: Int)(b: Int) = a + b`. Supplying the first list gives a function waiting for the rest: `val inc = add(1)` (in Scala 3 this eta-expands automatically). Multiple parameter lists also help type inference: in `foldLeft(0)(_ + _)` the type `Int` is fixed by the first list before the lambda is checked. A function value can be curried with `.curried` and uncurried with `Function.uncurried`.

Composition combines functions: `f andThen g` applies f then g, `f compose g` applies g then f.

**Partial functions** (`PartialFunction[A, B]`) are defined only for some inputs, written as a block of `case` clauses. `collect` uses them to filter and map in one step, and `isDefinedAt` checks whether an input is covered.

Prefer small **pure functions** (ones that only compute a result from their inputs and change nothing else) combined this way; they're easy to test.
concepts.code:
def multiplier(k: Int): Int => Int = x => x * k
val triple = multiplier(3)
println(triple(5))                               // 15

def add(a: Int)(b: Int): Int = a + b
val inc = add(1)
println(List(1, 2, 3).map(inc))                  // List(2, 3, 4)

val trim: String => String = _.trim
val shout: String => String = _.toUpperCase + "!"
println((trim andThen shout)("  hi "))           // HI!

def retry[A](times: Int)(action: => A): A =
  try action
  catch case e: Exception if times > 1 => retry(times - 1)(action)

var attempts = 0
val result = retry(3) { attempts += 1; if attempts < 3 then sys.error("fail") else "ok" }
println(s"$result after $attempts attempts")     // ok after 3 attempts

val parseEven: PartialFunction[String, Int] = {
  case s if s.toIntOption.exists(_ % 2 == 0) => s.toInt
}
println(List("2", "x", "7", "10").collect(parseEven))  // List(2, 10)
takeaways: Functions can take and return functions (closures capture values)
Multiple parameter lists enable currying and better type inference
`andThen`/`compose` chain functions
`collect` with a partial function filters and maps at once
pitfalls: Calling a partial function on an input it's not defined for, which throws MatchError; check isDefinedAt or use lift.

quiz.q: val f = (x: Int) => x + 1; val g = (x: Int) => x * 2. What is (f andThen g)(3)?
quiz.explain: andThen applies f first (3 + 1 = 4), then g (4 * 2 = 8).

concepts.name: Collections in depth: views and mutability
concepts.summary: Pick the right collection for performance, use views and LazyList for laziness, and use changeable (mutable) collections deliberately.
concepts.why: Choosing collections well matters for performance and memory in real workloads.
concepts.body:
The collections library is a hierarchy: `Iterable` at the top, then `Seq` (ordered, with `IndexedSeq` like `Vector`/`ArraySeq` and `LinearSeq` like `List`), `Set` and `Map`. Give parameters the most general type that fits (`Seq[A]`, `Iterable[A]`) so callers can pass any suitable collection, and pick the concrete one for its speed:

- `List`: instant to add at the front or split off the first item; slow to reach position n or add at the end (the time grows with the length).
- `Vector`: fast to read, update or add anywhere, however long it gets.
- `ArraySeq`/`Array`: compact and fastest for plain numbers; an `Array` can be changed in place.
- `HashMap`/`HashSet` are the defaults; `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` keep keys sorted; `ListMap` keeps insertion order but is slow (the default immutable `Map` keeps insertion order only up to 4 entries).

Chained operations like `xs.map(f).filter(p).take(10)` build an intermediate collection at each step. A **view** (`xs.view.map(f).filter(p).take(10).toList`) instead runs the steps item by item, only as far as needed: **lazy evaluation**. **LazyList** computes each item when first needed and then remembers it (**memoization**), so it can even be infinite; an `Iterator` hands out each item once and is then used up.

**Mutable** (changeable) collections (`scala.collection.mutable.ArrayBuffer`, `HashMap`, `ListBuffer`) are fine for local, performance-sensitive building; keep them private and expose immutable results (`buf.toList`). Importing `scala.jdk.CollectionConverters` adds `.asScala`/`.asJava` to convert to and from Java's collections.
concepts.code:
import scala.collection.mutable

val evens = LazyList.from(1).filter(_ % 2 == 0)
println(evens.take(5).toList)                   // List(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)

var calls = 0
val r = (1 to 1_000_000).view
  .map { x => calls += 1; x * x }
  .filter(_ % 7 == 0)
  .take(3)
  .toList
println(s"$r after $calls calls")               // List(49, 196, 441) after 21 calls

val buf = mutable.ArrayBuffer.empty[Int]
for i <- 1 to 5 do buf += i * 10
val frozen: Vector[Int] = buf.toVector          // expose immutable
println(frozen)                                 // Vector(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)

val counts = mutable.Map.empty[Char, Int].withDefaultValue(0)
"mississippi".foreach(c => counts(c) += 1)
println(counts.toSeq.sortBy(-_._2).head)        // (i,4) or (s,4)

val sorted = collection.immutable.TreeMap(3 -> "c", 1 -> "a", 2 -> "b")
println(sorted.keys.toList)                     // List(1, 2, 3)
takeaways: Code against Seq/Iterable; choose List, Vector or ArraySeq for performance
Views and LazyList avoid intermediate collections
Mutable collections for local building, immutable results outward
TreeMap for sorted keys; default Map order is not guaranteed
pitfalls: Relying on the iteration order of a default immutable Map or Set with more than four elements.

quiz.q: Why use .view before a chain of map/filter/take?
options: To avoid building intermediate collections and compute only what's needed
quiz.explain: A view fuses the operations lazily, so only the elements required by take are processed.

concepts.name: sbt projects and testing with MUnit
concepts.summary: Set up a project with build.sbt, add the libraries it needs with %%, and write tests with MUnit.
concepts.why: Real projects need a build, dependencies and tests; sbt is the most widely used Scala build tool.
concepts.body:
**sbt** is the standard Scala build tool. A minimal project is a `build.sbt` plus `project/build.properties` (which fixes the sbt version) and sources under `src/main/scala` and tests under `src/test/scala`. Type `sbt` once to open its interactive session, then run tasks inside it, which keeps the JVM running and fast between tasks: `compile`, `run`, `test`, `testOnly *ParserSuite`, `console` and `~test` (rerun on file changes).

The libraries a project needs, its **dependencies**, are listed as `"org" %% "name" % "version"`. The double `%%` adds the Scala version suffix (`_3`) to the name, picking the copy compiled for your Scala version; a single `%` is for plain Java libraries. Test-only libraries get `% Test`. A build with several sub-projects defines each with `lazy val core = project.in(file("core"))` and `dependsOn`.

Tests are code that checks your code. **MUnit** is a lightweight testing library that works with sbt and Scala CLI. A group of tests, a **test suite**, is a class that extends `munit.FunSuite` and declares `test("name") { ... }` blocks with `assertEquals(obtained, expected)`, `assert(cond)` and `intercept[Ex] { ... }`. When a check fails, it shows exactly how the actual value differs from the expected one. ScalaTest is the older, larger alternative, and ScalaCheck tries a rule against hundreds of generated inputs.

For single-file work, Scala CLI handles tests too: files ending in `.test.scala` with `//> using test.dep org.scalameta::munit::1.1.0` run with `scala test .`.
takeaways: build.sbt declares settings; run tasks inside an sbt session
`%%` picks the library copy built for your Scala version; `% Test` limits it to tests
MUnit: extend FunSuite, write `test(...)` with assertEquals
`~test` reruns tests on every save
pitfalls: Using a single % for a Scala library, which fails to find it or pulls in a copy built for another Scala version.

quiz.q: What does %% do in "org.scalameta" %% "munit" % "1.1.0"?
options: Appends the Scala binary version suffix to the artifact name
quiz.explain: %% resolves munit_3 for Scala 3 projects, matching the library build to your Scala version.

concepts.name: Generics, variance and bounds
concepts.summary: Write code that works for any type with type parameters, and control how such types relate with +A, -A and type bounds.
concepts.why: Type variance decides when, say, a list of cats can be used where a list of animals is expected.
concepts.body:
Classes, traits and methods can take **type parameters**, placeholders for types filled in when they are used: `class Box[A](value: A)`, `def first[A](xs: List[A]): Option[A]`. Code written this way is generic (**generics**), and the compiler usually works the types out at each call.

**Type variance** describes how the subtype relationship of the parameter carries over to the generic type. Write `Cat <: Animal` for "Cat is a subtype of Animal":

- **Covariant** `+A`: `List[Cat] <: List[Animal]`. Right for types that only hand values out and never change: `List`, `Option`, `Vector`, `Either`.
- **Contravariant** `-A`: `Printer[Animal] <: Printer[Cat]`. Right for consumers: a function that accepts any `Animal` can be used where one accepting `Cat` is needed. `Function1[-A, +B]` is contravariant in input and covariant in output.
- **Invariant** (no `+` or `-`): no relationship. Required for changeable (mutable) collections: `Array[Cat]` must not be an `Array[Animal]`, or you could put a `Dog` into it.

The compiler checks where `+A` and `-A` types appear: a covariant type can't appear as a method parameter. The fix is a **lower bound**, one kind of **type bound** (a limit on a type parameter): `def prepend[B >: A](b: B): List[B]` widens the element type as needed, which is how `List` lets you add an `Animal` to a `List[Cat]`.

**Upper bounds** `A <: Comparable[A]` restrict a parameter to subtypes. For capabilities like ordering, a type class (a separate description of the capability, `using Ordering[A]`, covered in the givens lesson) is often better, because it works for types you don't control.

Type parameters are removed when compiling for the JVM (**type erasure**): while the program runs, `List[Int]` and `List[String]` are the same class, so `case xs: List[Int]` can't be checked. A `ClassTag` or `TypeTest` recovers some information when needed.
concepts.code:
sealed trait Animal { def name: String }
case class Cat(name: String) extends Animal
case class Dog(name: String) extends Animal

final case class Box[+A](value: A):
  def map[B](f: A => B): Box[B] = Box(f(value))
  def orElse[B >: A](other: B): List[B] = List(value, other)  // lower bound

trait Printer[-A]:
  def print(a: A): String

val animalPrinter: Printer[Animal] = a => s"animal ${a.name}"
val catPrinter: Printer[Cat] = animalPrinter      // OK: contravariance

val catBox: Box[Cat] = Box(Cat("Tom"))
val animalBox: Box[Animal] = catBox               // OK: covariance
println(animalBox.map(_.name))                    // Box(Tom)
println(catBox.orElse(Dog("Rex")))                // List(Cat(Tom), Dog(Rex))
println(catPrinter.print(Cat("Kit")))             // animal Kit

def maxOf[A <: Comparable[A]](a: A, b: A): A = if a.compareTo(b) >= 0 then a else b
println(maxOf("pear", "apple"))                   // pear
// val arr: Array[Animal] = Array[Cat]()          // error: Array is invariant
takeaways: `+A` covariant for producers, `-A` contravariant for consumers, invariant for mutable
Use a lower bound `B >: A` to accept wider types in covariant classes
Upper bounds `A <: T` restrict; type classes are often better
Generics are erased at runtime
pitfalls: Matching `case xs: List[Int]` and expecting the element type to be checked; it's erased.

quiz.q: Why is Array invariant while List is covariant?
options: Arrays are mutable, so covariance would allow writing a Dog into an Array[Cat]
It's a historical accident with no reason
quiz.explain: Mutable containers both read and write elements, so only invariance is type-safe.

concepts.name: Givens, using clauses and type classes
concepts.summary: Let the compiler pass arguments for you: provide instances with given, ask for them with using, and build type classes.
concepts.why: Type classes power sorting rules, converting data to and from JSON text, number-like abstractions and every major functional library.
concepts.body:
Scala 3 **contextual abstractions** let the compiler pass arguments for you based on their type.

- A `given` defines a **given instance**, the standard value of some type for the compiler to use (an `Ordering` says how to sort): `given Ordering[Version] = Ordering.by(v => (v.major, v.minor))`.
- A **using clause** declares a parameter the compiler fills in from the givens visible at that point in the code: `def sortAll[A](xs: List[A])(using ord: Ordering[A])`. Callers write `sortAll(versions)`, or pass one explicitly with `sortAll(versions)(using reverseOrd)`.
- A **context bound** is shorthand: `def sortAll[A: Ordering](xs: List[A])`, and `summon[Ordering[A]]` retrieves the instance.

Together these implement **type classes**: a generic trait describing a capability (`trait Show[A] { def show(a: A): String }`), given instances for each type, and generic functions requiring the capability. Unlike inheritance, you can add a capability to types you don't own (`Int`, `java.time.Instant`) and choose different instances in different scopes.

Where does the compiler look? In the surrounding code, including what you've imported, and in the **implicit scope** of the types involved: companion objects of `Show`, of `A`, and of their parts. Put instances for your own types in their companions and they're found without imports. Importing givens needs the special form `import mylib.given`.

`derives Show` on a case class auto-generates an instance when the type class supports derivation.
concepts.code:
trait Show[A]:
  def show(a: A): String

object Show:
  given Show[Int] with
    def show(n: Int) = s"#$n"
  given [A](using s: Show[A]): Show[List[A]] with
    def show(xs: List[A]) = xs.map(s.show).mkString("[", ", ", "]")

case class Version(major: Int, minor: Int)
object Version:
  given Ordering[Version] = Ordering.by(v => (v.major, v.minor))
  given Show[Version] = v => s"v${v.major}.${v.minor}"

def describe[A: Show](a: A): String = "value " + summon[Show[A]].show(a)

@main def tc(): Unit =
  println(describe(42))                        // value #42
  println(describe(List(1, 2)))                // value [#1, #2]
  val vs = List(Version(1, 10), Version(1, 2), Version(0, 9))
  println(vs.sorted.map(describe(_)))          // List(value v0.9, value v1.2, value v1.10)
  println(vs.max)                              // Version(1,10)
  val newestFirst = summon[Ordering[Version]].reverse
  println(vs.sorted(using newestFirst).head)   // Version(1,10)
takeaways: `given` provides an instance; `using` requires one
Context bounds `[A: Show]` plus `summon` are shorthand
Type classes add capabilities to types you don't own
Companion objects are searched automatically; others need `import x.given`
pitfalls: Defining givens in an unrelated object and forgetting `import thatObject.given`; a normal import x.* doesn't bring givens.

quiz.q: Where should a given Ordering[Version] live so that it's found without imports?
options: In the companion object of Version
quiz.explain: The implicit scope of a type includes its companion object, so instances there are always found.

concepts.name: Extension methods
concepts.summary: Add methods to existing types with extension, and combine them with type classes for readable method-call style.
concepts.why: Extensions give readable method calls on types you don't control, without wrapper objects or inheritance.
concepts.body:
An **extension method** adds a method to a type after the fact:

```scala
extension (s: String) def words: List[String] = s.split("\\s+").toList
```

Now `"a b c".words` works anywhere the extension is visible. Several methods can share one clause with an indented block, type parameters are allowed (`extension [A](xs: List[A]) def second: Option[A]`), and operators can be defined too.

The compiler finds an extension when it's visible by name (defined or imported nearby) or when it's defined in a given instance or companion object in the implicit scope of the type being extended. This makes extensions a natural partner for **type classes**: define them inside the type class trait and every type with an instance gets the syntax:

```scala
trait Show[A]:
  extension (a: A) def show: String
```

Under the hood an extension is just a method with the receiver as an extra first parameter; no wrapper object is created, so it costs nothing while the program runs.

Extensions can't override existing methods: if the type already has a member with that name, the real member wins. Use them for convenience and domain-specific syntax, and keep them discoverable by putting them next to the types or type classes they extend.
concepts.code:
extension (s: String)
  def words: List[String] = s.trim.split("\\s+").toList
  def isPalindrome: Boolean =
    val c = s.toLowerCase.filter(_.isLetter)
    c == c.reverse

extension [A](xs: List[A])
  def second: Option[A] = xs.drop(1).headOption

case class Money(cents: Long)
extension (m: Money)
  def +(o: Money): Money = Money(m.cents + o.cents)
  def pretty: String = f"$$${m.cents / 100.0}%.2f"

trait Show[A]:
  extension (a: A) def show: String
given Show[Boolean] with
  extension (b: Boolean) def show = if b then "yes" else "no"

@main def ext(): Unit =
  println("  to be  or not ".words)           // List(to, be, or, not)
  println("Never odd or even".isPalindrome)   // true
  println(List(1, 2, 3).second)               // Some(2)
  println((Money(150) + Money(275)).pretty)   // $4.25
  println(true.show)                          // yes
takeaways: `extension (x: T) def m = ...` adds methods to existing types
Extensions inside type classes give syntax to every instance
No runtime wrapper: the receiver is just the first parameter
Existing members always take precedence
pitfalls: Defining an extension with the same name as an existing method and wondering why it's never called.

quiz.q: String already has a method trim. You define extension (s: String) def trim = "x". What does " a ".trim return?
quiz.explain: Real members take precedence over extensions, so String.trim runs.

concepts.name: Futures and asynchronous code
concepts.summary: Run work in the background with Future and ExecutionContext, combine the results and handle failures.
concepts.why: Programs that talk to networks and databases spend much of their time waiting, and do better waiting on several things at once; Future is Scala's built-in basic tool for that.
concepts.body:
A **Future** (`Future[A]`) is a value that will be available later, computed on a **thread pool**: a set of **threads**, each an independent line of work running alongside the others. `Future { work }` starts the work immediately on an **ExecutionContext** (the thread pool to use), which you supply as a `using` parameter; `scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext.Implicits.global` is a reasonable default for **CPU-bound** work, which is busy calculating rather than waiting.

Futures combine without **blocking**, that is, without making a thread sit idle while it waits:

- `map`, `flatMap` and `for` comprehensions chain dependent steps.
- `Future.sequence(list)` and `Future.traverse` turn many futures into one; `zip` combines two.
- `recover` and `recoverWith` handle failures; a failed future carries the exception, and later steps are skipped.
- `onComplete` registers a **callback**, code to run when the future finishes, which receives a `Try`.

Futures start working as soon as they are created (**eager evaluation**): two futures created before a `for` run in parallel (at the same time), while futures created inside it run one after the other. Start independent work first, then combine.

Never block inside a future-based service. `Await.result(f, 5.seconds)` exists for tests and the top of `main`; elsewhere return the `Future`. Wrap code that waits on files or the network in `blocking { ... }` so the global pool can add threads to make up for it.

Futures can't be cancelled, and creating one already starts the work, so a Future can't be treated as a plan to run later. Larger codebases often use **effect systems** such as Cats Effect or ZIO: libraries whose `IO` values describe work without starting it, adding cancellation, safe clean-up of files and connections, and tasks that can't outlive the task that started them. Java 21's virtual threads (very cheap threads) are a simpler alternative for code written in a waiting style.
concepts.code:
import scala.concurrent.{Future, Await, blocking}
import scala.concurrent.duration.*
import scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext.Implicits.global

def fetchPrice(item: String): Future[Double] = Future {
  blocking(Thread.sleep(200))                    // simulate blocking I/O
  if item == "unknown" then throw IllegalArgumentException(item)
  item.length * 1.5
}

val start = System.nanoTime
val fa = fetchPrice("apple")                     // both start now
val fb = fetchPrice("kiwi")
val total = for a <- fa; b <- fb yield a + b
println(Await.result(total, 2.seconds))          // 13.5
println((System.nanoTime - start) / 1_000_000 < 380)  // true: ran in parallel

val all = Future.traverse(List("fig", "plum"))(fetchPrice)
println(Await.result(all, 2.seconds))            // List(4.5, 6.0)

val safe = fetchPrice("unknown").recover { case _: IllegalArgumentException => 0.0 }
println(Await.result(safe, 2.seconds))           // 0.0
takeaways: `Future { ... }` starts immediately on an ExecutionContext
Compose with map/flatMap/for, traverse and recover
Create independent futures before the for comprehension to run them in parallel
Await only in tests and at the program edge
pitfalls: Creating futures inside a for comprehension and expecting them to run concurrently; each starts after the previous completes.

quiz.q: val r = for a <- Future(slowA()); b <- Future(slowB()) yield a + b. How do slowA and slowB run?
options: Sequentially: slowB's future is created only after slowA completes
Not at all until Await is called
quiz.explain: The second Future is created inside flatMap's callback, so it starts only when the first finishes.

concepts.name: Java interoperability
concepts.summary: Use Java libraries from Scala, convert collections, handle Java's null values and make Scala code usable from Java.
concepts.why: The whole JVM ecosystem is available to Scala, but the seams need care.
concepts.body:
Scala compiles to JVM **bytecode**, the same instructions Java compiles to, so any Java library is usable directly: `import java.time.LocalDate` and call methods as usual. Java classes are created without `new` in Scala 3 too, Java static methods (methods that belong to the class itself, not to an instance) are called on the class name, and Java getters work with or without parentheses.

The seams to watch:

- **Collections**: Java and Scala collections are different types. `import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters.*` adds `.asScala` and `.asJava`, which wrap without copying.
- **Null**: Java methods may return `null`, a "no value" that crashes the program if used as a real value. Wrap results with `Option(javaCall())`. (The `-Yexplicit-nulls` compiler flag makes the compiler track which Java values may be null.)
- **Functional interfaces**: an **interface** is Java's list of methods a class promises to provide, and one with a single method, like `Runnable`, `Comparator` or `java.util.function.Function`, is called functional. Scala lambdas convert to them automatically. `scala.jdk.FunctionConverters` and `scala.jdk.FutureConverters` cover other conversions, and `scala.jdk.OptionConverters` handles `java.util.Optional`.
- Java's **checked exceptions** (errors a Java method must declare it may throw) don't exist in Scala; use `@throws[IOException]` to declare them for Java callers.
- **Varargs**: annotate with `@varargs` to make a Scala varargs method callable from Java naturally.

Calling Scala from Java is possible but less pleasant: `object` members are reached through generated static methods, default parameters aren't visible, and Scala collections look odd. For libraries used from Java, add a thin Java-friendly layer on top.
concepts.code:
import java.time.{LocalDate, DayOfWeek}
import java.util.ArrayList
import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters.*
import scala.jdk.OptionConverters.*

val d = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 17)
println(d.getDayOfWeek)                          // SATURDAY
println(d.plusDays(2).getDayOfWeek == DayOfWeek.MONDAY)  // true

val jl = ArrayList[String]()
jl.add("pear"); jl.add("fig")
val sl: List[String] = jl.asScala.toList
println(sl.map(_.toUpperCase))                   // List(PEAR, FIG)

jl.sort((a: String, b: String) => a.length - b.length)  // lambda -> Comparator
println(jl)                                      // [fig, pear]

val props = System.getProperties
println(Option(props.getProperty("no.such.key")).getOrElse("default"))  // default
println(java.util.Optional.of(5).toScala)        // Some(5)
println(sl.asJava.isInstanceOf[java.util.List[?]])  // true (a wrapper, no copy)
takeaways: Java classes are used directly; static methods via the class name
`scala.jdk.CollectionConverters` adds `.asScala`/`.asJava` wrappers
Wrap possibly-null Java results in `Option(...)`
Lambdas convert to Java functional interfaces automatically
pitfalls: Passing a Scala List to a Java method expecting java.util.List without `.asJava`.

quiz.q: How do you safely handle a Java method that may return null?
quiz.explain: Option(x) becomes None for null and Some(x) otherwise; Some(null) would keep the null.

concepts.name: Opaque, union and intersection types
concepts.summary: Zero-cost type wrappers with opaque types, and precise types with A | B and A & B.
concepts.why: These Scala 3 features describe your data precisely, at no cost while the program runs.
concepts.body:
An **opaque type** is the underlying type while the program runs, but a separate type for the compiler. Inside the object that defines it, the two are interchangeable; outside, only the methods you provide are visible:

```scala
object ids:
  opaque type UserId = Long
  object UserId { def apply(n: Long): UserId = n }
```

`UserId` and `Long` can't be mixed up, yet no wrapper object is created, unlike a case class wrapper (and unlike Scala 2's value classes, which still get wrapped, or **boxed**, in generic code). Add operations with extension methods in the same scope, and use the companion to validate (`def from(n: Long): Option[UserId]`).

**Union types** `A | B` say "a value of type A or B". No wrapper is involved, and A and B needn't share a supertype: `def parse(s: String): Int | ParseError`. Pattern matching narrows them. Unions also let you list the exact values allowed (literal types): `type Dir = "N" | "S" | "E" | "W"`.

**Intersection types** `A & B` are values that are both: `def save(x: Serializable & Validated)`. They replace Scala 2's compound `with` types and are commutative (`A & B` equals `B & A`).

When inferring the type of a `val` or `def`, the compiler widens a union to a common non-union supertype: `val x = if c then 1 else "a"` doesn't get `Int | String` unless you annotate it, so write the union type where you want one. Opaque types can't be distinguished at runtime, so matching `case id: UserId` is an unchecked type test.
concepts.code:
object units:
  opaque type Meters = Double
  opaque type Seconds = Double
  def meters(d: Double): Meters = d
  def seconds(d: Double): Seconds = d
  extension (m: Meters) def /(s: Seconds): Double = m / s  // inside: Doubles
import units.*
val speed = meters(100) / seconds(9.58)
println(f"$speed%.2f m/s")                  // 10.44 m/s
// meters(1) / 2.0                          // error: found Double, required Seconds
enum ParseError { case Empty, Bad }
def parse(s: String): Int | ParseError =
  if s.isEmpty then ParseError.Empty else s.toIntOption.getOrElse(ParseError.Bad)

for s <- List("42", "", "x") do
  parse(s) match
    case n: Int        => println(s"int $n")
    case e: ParseError => println(s"error $e")   // int 42 / error Empty / error Bad
type Dir = "N" | "S"
val d: Dir = "N"                            // "W" would not compile
trait Named { def name: String }
trait Aged { def age: Int }
def card(p: Named & Aged) = s"${p.name} (${p.age})"
println(card(new Named with Aged { val name = "Ana"; val age = 31 }))  // Ana (31)
takeaways: Opaque types: distinct at compile time, the raw type at runtime
Add operations to opaque types with extensions in their scope
`A | B` unions need no common supertype; match to narrow
`A & B` values satisfy both types
pitfalls: Expecting the compiler to infer `Int | String` for an if/else: annotate the expected union type.

quiz.q: What is the runtime representation of opaque type UserId = Long?
quiz.explain: Opaque types erase to their underlying type, so there's no allocation overhead.

concepts.name: Inline and macros
concepts.summary: Compile-time programming with inline, compiletime ops, quotes and splices.
concepts.why: Libraries use these for helpers that cost nothing while the program runs, for generating type-class instances automatically and for checks during compiling.
concepts.body:
Scala 3 has a principled metaprogramming system built in layers.

**`inline`** is the first layer. An `inline def` (an **inline method**) is guaranteed to have its body copied into each place that calls it. Combined with `inline` parameters, `inline if` and `inline match`, the branches are resolved during compilation, so code specialised to fixed values costs nothing while the program runs. `transparent inline` methods may even return a more specific type than declared.

`scala.compiletime` adds tools usable inside inline code: `error("msg")` emits a custom compile error, `constValue[T]` turns a type standing for a fixed value, like `3`, back into that value, `erasedValue[T]` lets you match on types, and `summonInline`/`summonFrom` look up givens at expansion time. This is enough for a lot of type-class **derivation** with `scala.deriving.Mirror`.

**Macros** are the second layer: code that runs inside the compiler and writes code. An inline method calls `${ impl('x) }`, and `impl` is a regular method running in the compiler that receives typed code as `Expr[T]` and returns new code built with **quotes** `'{ ... }` and **splices** `${ ... }`. Macros are type-checked, hygienic (names they generate can't clash with yours) and, unlike Scala 2 macros, part of the stable language. The **reflection API** (`quotes.reflect`) gives full access to the code's tree structure when quotes aren't enough.

Rules: a macro implementation must be defined in a different file (compiled earlier) than its call sites, and macros can't introduce new definitions visible to the user's code. Use inline first and reach for macros only when you need to inspect or generate code.
takeaways: `inline` guarantees inlining; `inline if/match` resolve at compile time
`scala.compiletime` gives error, constValue and erasedValue
